courseInfo.scenarioTitle: Near-Fatal Asthma (Status Asthmaticus) With Impending Respiratory Failure
courseInfo.targetLearnerGroup: ED residents/registrars, ED nurses, respiratory therapists (if applicable), paramedics transitioning to ED
courseInfo.prerequisiteKnowledge: Adult asthma exacerbation assessment, initial ED stabilization (ABC), bronchodilator delivery, steroid therapy, magnesium use, escalation pathways (NIV/intubation), ventilator principles for severe asthma, closed-loop communication

objectives: Perform rapid initial assessment and stabilization of severe asthma using an ABC approach with early oxygenation, bronchodilators, and systemic corticosteroids.
Recognize signs of impending respiratory failure (fatigue, decreased air movement, rising CO2, altered mental status) and escalate care early (senior help/ICU/anesthesia).
Deliver evidence-based therapies for severe asthma exacerbation, including continuous inhaled bronchodilators, anticholinergic therapy, and IV magnesium sulfate when indicated.
Demonstrate safe preparation for ventilatory support (NIV trial when appropriate; RSI planning for difficult ventilation/air trapping) with clear role assignment and closed-loop communication.
Apply asthma-friendly ventilation principles after intubation (low rate, long expiratory time, avoid breath stacking, permissive hypercapnia) and manage complications (hypotension/auto-PEEP).
Provide a structured ICU handover including clinical trajectory, treatments given, response, and ongoing risks/monitoring needs.

clinicalSetting.remarks: SimMan in ED bed with wall oxygen, suction, monitor/defib available. Nebulizer setup and airway cart present.

instructors: Second instructor/assistant (voice of patient or consultant voice; optional)
confederates: ED triage/primary nurse (optional confederate to prompt workflow)
Respiratory therapist (optional confederate to assist with nebs/NIV/ventilator setup)

patientInfo.name: Jordan Parker
patientInfo.pastMedicalAndSocialHistory: Asthma since childhood with prior ICU admission (no prior intubations per family). Frequent SABA use; inconsistent inhaled corticosteroid use due to access issues. Seasonal allergies. No known cardiac disease. Non-smoker. Occasional cannabis vaping (last use yesterday).
patientInfo.currentMedications: Salbutamol (albuterol) inhaler PRN (using repeatedly today), budesonide/formoterol (inconsistent).
patientInfo.presentingComplaintHistory: Severe shortness of breath and wheeze for 8 hours, worsening over last 2 hours. Trigger: viral URI symptoms x 2 days. Used SABA >10 puffs today with minimal relief. Arrives anxious, speaking in short phrases, using accessory muscles.

scenarioInfo.scenarioSummary: A 34-year-old male with known asthma presents to the ED in severe respiratory distress after a viral prodrome and heavy SABA use. Despite initial bronchodilators and oxygen, he develops fatigue, rising CO2, and decreased air movement. Learners must recognize impending respiratory failure, escalate therapy, coordinate team roles, and implement safe ventilatory support (NIV trial if appropriate or RSI with asthma-friendly ventilation). Scenario emphasizes avoiding breath stacking/auto-PEEP, managing post-intubation hypotension, and providing a clear ICU handover.
scenarioInfo.scenarioInformationToTrainees: You are working in an ED resuscitation bay. A 34-year-old with known asthma has arrived in severe respiratory distress. Manage as you would in your department with available staff and resources.
scenarioInfo.transitionMode: Dynamic progression based on timely interventions and reassessment; instructor may accelerate deterioration if delays occur.

scenarioFlow.stateName: State 1: Arrival - Severe Asthma Exacerbation (Status Asthmaticus)
physicalExam: Patient upright, anxious, speaking 1-3 word phrases
Accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions
Prolonged expiratory phase, diffuse expiratory wheeze
Heart Sound: Gallop (optional; may omit if distracting)
Lung Sound: Wheezes
Pulses rapid, skin warm/diaphoretic
investigations: ABG/VBG available on request (initial): pH 7.33, pCO2 48, pO2 62, HCO3 24 (suggest early fatigue/rising CO2)
expectedActions: Assign roles; use closed-loop communication; place patient on monitor and obtain full set of vitals
Administer oxygen to target SpO2 94-98%
Establish IV access; draw labs as per local practice
Start inhaled bronchodilators: continuous nebulized SABA with ipratropium (or back-to-back nebs)
Administer systemic corticosteroid early (e.g., IV methylprednisolone or PO/IV equivalent)
Consider IV magnesium sulfate for severe exacerbation
Frequent reassessment of work of breathing, ability to speak, air entry, SpO2, and mental status
remarks: Capability: Spontaneous breathing
Capability: Bilateral chest rise and fall
Capability: Difficulty breathing
Capability: Cough
Capability: Moaning
Capability: IV Access (Right Arm Only)
If learners delay bronchodilators/steroids >3-4 minutes, worsen sooner (move to State 2 with more severe values).
If appropriate treatment initiated promptly, patient shows slight improvement in SpO2 but remains high risk; still progresses due to severe bronchospasm.
instructorControl: Provide patient voice: anxious, can only speak short phrases; endorses frequent inhaler use and URTI symptoms
Cue nurse/confederate to ask: 'Should we start continuous nebs and get magnesium ready?' if team stalls
If asked about history: no anaphylaxis signs; no fever; chest tightness without pleuritic pain
If learners ask about prior episodes: 'ICU once a few years ago; never intubated'
scenarioFlow.transitionRule: After initial treatments are started and 3-5 minutes elapse OR if there is a delay in escalation, transition to State 2 (worsening/fatigue).

scenarioFlow.stateName: State 2: Deterioration - Fatigue and Rising CO2 Despite Initial Therapy
physicalExam: More fatigued; less agitated; still severe distress
Speech: single words or nodding only
Air entry reduced bilaterally; wheeze less prominent
Lung Sound: Wheezes (diminishing) with areas of poor air movement
Diaphoresis; tired appearance
Possible paradoxical breathing if learners assess closely
investigations: VBG/ABG if ordered now: pH 7.25, pCO2 62, pO2 70 (on oxygen), HCO3 27
CXR (if ordered): hyperinflation; no focal consolidation; no pneumothorax
Electrolytes (if asked): mild hypokalemia possible after beta-agonists
expectedActions: Recognize impending respiratory failure (fatigue, rising CO2, reduced air movement)
Escalate bronchodilator delivery (ensure continuous nebulization and adequate dosing) and confirm steroids and magnesium given
Consider epinephrine (IM) if life-threatening asthma with poor air movement (per local protocol) or consider ketamine as an adjunct for severe bronchospasm (per local practice)
Prepare for ventilatory support: call for senior help/anesthesia/ICU, prepare airway equipment, assign airway and medication roles
Consider noninvasive ventilation if appropriate and patient cooperative; monitor closely for failure
Optimize positioning, minimize agitation, avoid excessive sedation unless preparing for definitive airway management
remarks: Capability: Spontaneous breathing
Capability: Difficulty breathing

If learners appropriately escalate early and prepare, the patient may stabilize briefly before near-fatal decline; if they fail to recognize danger, rapid progression to State 3 with altered mental status.

If learners attempt intubation without preparation for difficult ventilation/air trapping, make BVM ventilation challenging (high resistance), requiring corrective actions (two-person BVM, airway adjuncts, slower ventilation).
instructorControl: If learners ask about compliance: admits not taking controller inhaler regularly
If learners request consultant: ICU says 'Prepare for possible intubation; we can accept once stabilized'
If NIV attempted: initial tolerance is poor unless team coaches; if coached, SpO2 improves modestly but CO2 continues to rise (failure over minutes)
If learners ask about mental status: 'He looks more tired and is less responsive to questions'
scenarioFlow.transitionRule: Transition to State 3 when learners either (a) miss signs of impending failure for 2-3 minutes, or (b) despite appropriate therapy, ABG shows worsening hypercapnia and patient becomes altered/exhausted.

scenarioFlow.stateName: State 3: Near-Fatal Asthma - Silent Chest, Altered Mental Status
physicalExam: Drowsy, poor cooperation; cannot speak
Minimal air movement bilaterally ('silent chest')
Lung Sound: Absent breath sounds
Cooler extremities; diaphoresis persists
Weak peripheral pulses
investigations: ABG/VBG now: pH 7.10, pCO2 90, pO2 58 (on oxygen), HCO3 28
ETCO2 if available after assisted ventilation: elevated with prolonged expiratory phase waveform (if team uses capnography post-intubation)
expectedActions: Declare impending respiratory arrest; activate additional resources (airway/ICU/anesthesia) and prepare for immediate airway intervention
Optimize pre-oxygenation as feasible and prepare for difficult ventilation (two-person bag-mask, airway adjuncts)
Perform RSI only when ready for high-resistance ventilation; confirm tube placement clinically and with CO2 detection
After intubation: implement asthma-friendly ventilation strategy (low rate, long expiratory time, avoid breath stacking; permissive hypercapnia as needed)
Continue bronchodilators via inline nebulization (if available), continue steroids; consider adjuncts per local protocol
Monitor for hypotension after positive pressure ventilation; treat with fluids/vasopressors as needed and reduce auto-PEEP by adjusting ventilation
remarks: Capability: Bag-mask ventilation
Capability: Intubation
Capability: Suctioning
Capability: Palpation of pulses
If learners ventilate too fast/high tidal volumes, SpO2 and BP worsen (simulate dynamic hyperinflation/auto-PEEP) and ETCO2 rises; prompt them to slow rate and allow full exhalation.
If learners do not proceed to definitive airway/ventilation, patient progresses toward peri-arrest (optional instructor decision).
instructorControl: Make BVM ventilation initially difficult (high resistance); improvement occurs with correct technique: two-person seal, airway adjunct, slower ventilation, adequate expiratory time
If intubated: confirm with rising CO2 and bilateral chest rise; lung sounds remain very quiet initially
If learners request 'manual disconnect' concept due to air trapping: allow improvement in BP/SpO2 after brief disconnect and slower ventilation (teach point)
If learners give adequate sedation/analgesia post-intubation (verbalized), allow improved synchrony; if not, patient 'bucks' (instructor cue) and SpO2/BP worsen until managed
scenarioFlow.transitionRule: Transition to State 4 after appropriate airway/ventilation strategy is implemented and team corrects breath stacking (or after effective NIV/assisted ventilation with clear improvement).

scenarioFlow.stateName: State 4: Stabilization - Improved Oxygenation and Ventilation After Correct Management
physicalExam: If intubated: sedated, synchronized with ventilator; chest rise present with slower respiratory pattern
Air movement improving; wheeze may return as airflow improves
Lung Sound: Wheezes (mild/moderate) or improving air entry
Skin color improves; diaphoresis decreases
No external bleeding; no rash/urticaria
investigations: Repeat ABG/VBG (after stabilization): pH 7.22, pCO2 70, pO2 90 (improving oxygenation; permissive hypercapnia acceptable early)
Electrolytes: monitor K+/Mg2+ if beta-agonist heavy use
expectedActions: Reassess and document response to interventions and trends
Maintain ongoing bronchodilator therapy and steroids; continue supportive care
Communicate plan and disposition (ICU admission) with clear handover (situation, background, assessment, recommendation)
Anticipate complications (hypotension, barotrauma, dysrhythmias, hypokalemia) and monitor appropriately
Provide family communication if applicable and time allows
remarks: If learners demonstrate strong ICU handover and appropriate ongoing management, scenario can end here.
If learners omit ongoing bronchodilators/steroids, allow mild re-worsening to reinforce continuous therapy and reassessment (optional).
Avoid making this a tension pneumothorax case unless learners specifically perform interventions that warrant that complication.
instructorControl: If asked about ventilator strategy, confirm that slower rate and longer expiratory time improved BP/SpO2 and reduced breath stacking
Provide ICU acceptance once stable: 'We’ll take the patient—please send ABG trends and meds given'
If learners ask for a brief disconnect: allow rapid BP improvement to reinforce concept
scenarioFlow.transitionRule: End scenario when learners have stabilized the patient, articulated ongoing management, and arranged ICU-level care.

scenarioFlow.stateName: State 5: Stabilization - Improved Oxygenation and Ventilation After Correct Management
physicalExam: If intubated: sedated, synchronized with ventilator; chest rise present with slower respiratory pattern
Air movement improving; wheeze may return as airflow improves
Lung Sound: Wheezes (mild/moderate) or improving air entry
Skin color improves; diaphoresis decreases
investigations: Repeat ABG/VBG (after stabilization): pH 7.22, pCO2 70, pO2 90 (improving oxygenation; permissive hypercapnia acceptable early)

expectedActions: Reassess and document response to interventions and trends

Set Lung Sound: Wheezes initially; reduce air movement over time; switch to Lung Sound: Absent breath sounds in near-fatal state
Enable Capability: Spontaneous breathing, Bilateral chest rise and fall, Difficulty breathing, Cough, Moaning
Prepare transition to assisted ventilation with Capability: Bag-mask ventilation and Capability: Intubation
